questions.title: When and why do the drawings move?
questions.why_it_matters: It decides what the match timer, the countdown and the hidden score mean in the world.

options.name: Away From The Desk
options.pitch: The person draws the scene, picks up a mug and walks off. The drawings come alive when the chair is empty and freeze when footsteps return.
options.gives: The timer is how long they are gone, and the reveal is them sitting back down. The score stays hidden because nobody is watching.
options.costs: It is the most familiar option, and the cursor has to stay parked on screen to keep core idea 3.
options.moment: A door clicks offscreen and everyone snaps back into their drawn pose mid-stride.

options.name: Only While Unsaved
options.pitch: The drawings live only while the title bar shows an unsaved mark. The match lasts until the person saves.
options.gives: A tidy reason for the timer and the end: saving locks the winning colour into the slot.
options.costs: You barely see it during play. It explains the start and end of a match, not the middle.
options.moment: The crude title-bar asterisk blinks faster, then a wobbly 'Saving...' box locks the paint in.

options.name: Not Responding
options.pitch: The drawing program hangs and the window goes grey. While it is frozen, the drawings break loose. The match ends when it recovers.
options.gives: It explains the grey world: the hung window washes everything out, and only living paint keeps its colour.
options.costs: The hang screen has to be invented so it looks like no real OS, and a crash is a little less cosy as a premise.
options.moment: A crude 'This program is thinking...' box sits greyed out over the arena while the war rages underneath.

options.name: Stuck At The Colour Picker
options.pitch: The person is at the desk with the colour picker open, unable to choose between two swatches. While they dither, the teams fight to decide for them.
options.gives: It is the most direct link to core idea 2: every match is that moment of indecision.
options.costs: The same decision comes up every match, so it needs a running gag about them changing their mind.
options.moment: The giant cursor wobbles between the orange and blue swatches as the lead changes.

options.name: Freeze When Watched
options.pitch: The drawings are always alive, but anything near the cursor must hold still. The person is idly moving the mouse and noticing nothing.
options.gives: The human is in the match the whole time as a wandering hazard, not just at the start and end.
options.costs: It is a real mechanic, so it needs building and tuning, and could feel random in split-screen.
options.moment: The arrow drifts over the hill and four box-heads lock into silly poses until it slides away.

options.name: The Person Is In On It
options.pitch: The drawings are alive and the person knows it. Unable to fill the empty slot, they let the drawings settle it and referee with the cursor.
options.gives: The boldest option: the cursor can openly hand out weapons, start modes and announce the reveal.
options.costs: It loses the secret-life charm, and the person must stay a gesture, not a mascot.
options.moment: The cursor drags a crude bucket out of the toolbar and drops it in front of a box-head, who tips his cap.

questions.title: Why do the box-heads care who gets the slot?
questions.why_it_matters: It gives the players' figures a want, and the strongest options also explain a mechanic.

options.name: It's Just Their Team
options.pitch: They were drawn in that colour's cap and overalls, so that is their side, like a footballer and their shirt. The slot is the trophy.
options.gives: No story to maintain, and nothing to explain beyond blue against orange.
options.costs: The box-heads get no inner life, and the slot becomes set dressing.
options.moment: The cursor tints each cap with one bucket click, and the teams start glaring at each other.

options.name: Copy-Pasted Rivals
options.pitch: Both teams are the same box-head, copied and pasted, and each insists it is the original. Winning the slot proves who came first.
options.gives: A petty, funny motive that explains why the teams look identical apart from their colour.
options.costs: It is a joke more than a stake, with no way to escalate it.
options.moment: The cursor scrawls 'original' over the winners, and both teams point at it.

options.name: They Want To Be Coloured In
options.pitch: The figures are unfinished outlines. Whichever colour takes the slot is what the person will fill them in with, so winning means finally being coloured.
options.gives: A warm, sympathetic want, and the grey world means something: everything is waiting for its fill.
options.costs: The losers stay grey, which needs a light touch to stay funny and not sad.
options.moment: The bucket cursor clicks each winner once, and they flood with colour and admire their overalls.

options.name: Running On Their Own Ink
options.pitch: The figures are made of their team's paint and the palette well is their only refill. Every shot spends a bit of themselves.
options.gives: It explains ammo, refilling and why paint matters physically.
options.costs: It is the most mechanical option and can read as survival instead of a joke.
options.moment: A player who sprays too long drains to a grey outline and slurps colour back from their own puddle.

options.name: Losers Get Redrawn Worse
options.pitch: Nobody dies. A splatted figure is rubbed out and redrawn quickly and badly, so you come back wonkier.
options.gives: It explains respawning and puts a comic threat behind losing.
options.costs: Erasing has to stay silly, and the wonky redraws need a little extra art.
options.moment: A box-head respawns in three hurried strokes, one eye bigger and cap sideways, shrugs, and runs back in.

options.name: Make It Onto The Fridge
options.pitch: The person will keep the picture in the winning colour, pinned up or saved. The losing version is an unsaved change, and both teams want to be the one that is kept.
options.gives: A warm want, being remembered, that ties the hidden score to the person coming back.
options.costs: It needs an invented 'keep it' beat, a frame or a print, that looks like no real OS.
options.moment: The canvas shrinks into a crude frame and the winners pose stiffly inside it.

questions.title: What are the two colours, really?
questions.why_it_matters: It explains the random colour pairs and whether the colours are characters or just prizes.

options.name: Just Two Colours
options.pitch: The colours are only colours and nobody is behind them. The slot is the prize.
options.gives: Nothing to explain, write or draw.
options.costs: The teams have no personality, so the core ideas carry all the charm.
options.moment: The slot fills with the winner while the loser slides off its edge.

options.name: The Person Couldn't Decide
options.pitch: The person narrowed the slot down to two colours and never chose. Each random pair is a different day's indecision.
options.gives: It explains the random pairs and the single slot in one line.
options.costs: The colours are passive, so all the drama comes from the box-heads.
options.moment: The cursor sits frozen between two swatches, and the match decides which one it would have clicked.

options.name: One Colour, Split In Two
options.pitch: The person dragged one colour toward the slot and the program glitched it into two opposite halves. Each half wants to be the whole colour again.
options.gives: It explains why the pairs are near-opposites and turns the fight into a family squabble.
options.costs: Blue/yellow is not a true complementary pair, and the glitch is one more invented event.
options.moment: A crude colour wheel cracks down the middle and the halves drop onto opposite spawns.

options.name: Eyedropped From The Room
options.pitch: The person used the eyedropper on things off the screen, their mug and their jumper. The colours are samples of the real room.
options.gives: It ties the colours to the human and gives each pair a cheap, funny origin.
options.costs: Each pair needs matching real-world objects and a little menu art.
options.moment: Team select shows a crude eyedropper pulling blue off a doodled mug and orange off a sleeve.

options.name: A Gift For The Person
options.pitch: Each team is sure the person will love the picture best in their colour. The slot holds the one they will see when they come back.
options.gives: The fight becomes a kind one: two crews competing to please the same person.
options.costs: Devotion to the person can turn sentimental without a light touch.
options.moment: After the reveal everyone freezes in place, beaming, as the cursor twitches back to life.

options.name: Paint As A Pet
options.pitch: Each colour is a happy, blobby puddle the box-heads let off the leash. It just wants to spread.
options.gives: Painting reads as letting something happy run loose, not as war.
options.costs: It adds a creature to draw that competes with the box-heads for attention.
options.moment: A bucket throw lands and the paint wags as it spreads.

questions.title: Who is the person at the computer?
questions.why_it_matters: It sets the warmth and tone of core idea 3, and how much of a character the player is asked to love.

options.name: Nobody, Only The Cursor
options.pitch: There is never a person, only an arrow that sometimes twitches. Whether anyone is there is never asked.
options.gives: Costs nothing and keeps all three core ideas with no story to maintain.
options.costs: There is no human to get attached to.
options.moment: In a long silence the cursor jumps an inch and all eight dot-eyes turn to look.

options.name: Called Away For Dinner
options.pitch: Your Toy Story idea, kept small. A kid draws the scene, gets called for dinner, and the drawings fight until they come back.
options.gives: The timer is how long dinner takes, and the score is hidden because nobody is there to see it.
options.costs: It is the obvious reading and Toy Story owns it, so it needs one twist of its own.
options.moment: With ten seconds left, a speech bubble from off the canvas reads 'COMING!' and everyone paints twice as fast.

options.name: The Lunch-Break Doodle
options.pitch: An office worker sketches the little guys on their lunch break and goes off for a sandwich. A match is one lunch hour.
options.gives: Adult, relatable comedy, and the grey world fits: a dull work file where the team colours are the only fun.
options.costs: Office humour can tip into bleakness.
options.moment: The results screen is a crude clock at 1:00 and a mug clunks down at the edge of the frame.

options.name: Fell Asleep At The Desk
options.pitch: Whoever drew this nodded off with a hand on the mouse. They know nothing, but their sleeping hand moves the world.
options.gives: Twitches explain Turbulence and cursor hazards, and waking up is the reveal.
options.costs: Being asleep every match could get samey unless each stage twitches differently.
options.moment: A 'Zzz' drifts across the canvas, then the cursor jerks and drags a grey stripe through orange's best turf.

options.name: Grandad Takes The Credit
options.pitch: A grandparent is slowly learning the computer. They keep coming back to a finished picture and, delighted, assume they did it.
options.gives: The warmest option: the reveal is a proud 'I did that!', and a slow, careful cursor is funny on its own.
options.costs: Jokes must stay about care, not confusion or decline.
options.moment: The slot fills, and a wobbly cursor double-clicks it three times before typing 'lovely' in the corner.

options.name: The Person Is You
options.pitch: The person at the computer is the players. The menu cursor is your hand, and starting a match means stepping away.
options.gives: Menus and matches become one fiction, and core idea 3 needs no extra art.
options.costs: It is abstract. The warmth has to come from the drawings reacting to you.
options.moment: Your menu cursor reappears at the end and the drawings scramble back to their places, one still caught mid-paint.

questions.title: What does the cursor do during a match?
questions.why_it_matters: It decides whether the human is a background detail, a sound, a clock or part of the level.

options.name: The Parked Arrow
options.pitch: The cursor sits where the person left it, half off a ledge, for the whole match. It never moves.
options.gives: It shows that someone is real and has stepped away, for almost no cost.
options.costs: Players stop noticing it after one match.
options.moment: A crude white arrow sits in a corner like a sleeping cat while fights rage below it.

options.name: Heard, Never Seen
options.pitch: The cursor stays idle and the person is only sound from another room: a kettle, a creaking chair, footsteps. A door ends the match.
options.gives: The end of the match becomes the person coming back, and nothing new has to be drawn.
options.costs: It leans entirely on audio, and a fresh clone is silent.
options.moment: With ten seconds left the footsteps get louder, and the last spray goes off over a creaking chair.

options.name: Busy Cursor Countdown
options.pitch: At the start the cursor is a lumpy, invented busy spinner. When it turns back into an arrow, the drawings can move.
options.gives: The start countdown happens in the world.
options.costs: It only covers three seconds, so another idea has to carry the rest.
options.moment: Four frozen box-heads under a wobbling spinner burst into motion as it becomes an arrow.

options.name: Screensaver Clock
options.pitch: The timer is how long until the idle screen goes to sleep. The screen dims near the end, and the person wiggles the mouse to wake it for the reveal.
options.gives: It explains the match length and why nobody sees the score until the end.
options.costs: In four-way split-screen the dimming has to stay a soft tint.
options.moment: The world sinks into blue-grey dusk, then the arrow jerks and the screen snaps bright.

options.name: The Drifting Arrow
options.pitch: Something is nudging the mouse, a cat or a sleeve, so the arrow slowly crosses the level as a solid object you can ride or get shoved by.
options.gives: The person becomes a moving platform, which suits Turbulence and the Movement Course.
options.costs: It needs collision tuning and may feel random on competitive stages.
options.moment: A player rides the arrow's tip across a gap, spraying downward, until it lurches and dumps them.

options.name: Notes Left Behind
options.pitch: Before leaving, the person typed crude, misspelled notes onto the canvas, like 'brb dont touch'. The letters are solid ground.
options.gives: It gives the person a voice and builds stages out of their words.
options.costs: Every stage needs its own lettering and collision, and the jokes go stale if the notes never change.
options.moment: Players fight over a King of the Hill perched on a lopsided 'brb' whose letters fill pink and green.

questions.title: How is the slot decided, and what is the reveal?
questions.why_it_matters: The reveal is the one moment the hidden score becomes visible, so it is where the premise pays off.

options.name: Recent Colours Shuffle
options.pitch: The program keeps a recent-colours strip sorted by use. At the whistle the two swatches jostle, and the one that covered more slides into the slot.
options.gives: The smallest answer: just software doing what software does, mapped exactly to area.
options.costs: The person has no part in it unless the cursor clicks OK afterwards.
options.moment: Two swatches nudge each other like people in a queue, a pixel counter flickers, and one pops in with a 'tink'.

options.name: Zoom To Fit
options.pitch: The person zooms all the way out. Each step averages the paint into chunkier pixels until the whole arena is one pixel, and that colour fills the slot.
options.gives: Squinting at the picture becomes the scoring, and you watch territory merge step by step.
options.costs: Averaging can turn muddy, so the last step has to snap to the nearer team.
options.moment: A 2x2 grid of blue and orange becomes a single block that wobbles between the two, then settles on orange.

options.name: The Cursor Dithers
options.pitch: The person reaches for a swatch but wavers, pulled toward whichever colour covers more. It drifts, doubts and clicks.
options.gives: It keeps the human in charge and puts all the suspense in one readable object.
options.costs: The pull has to be visibly proportional, or it looks random.
options.moment: The arrow creeps toward pink, darts to green, hovers, clicks green, and the green team throws their caps.

options.name: Save With Three Colours
options.pitch: The invented file format holds only grey, black and one more. Saving sweeps a progress bar across the map and turns the losing colour grey.
options.gives: It explains the world: the grey is every losing team's paint, ever.
options.costs: Watching your paint go grey stings, so the sweep must be quick and jaunty.
options.moment: A chunky progress bar crawls across, the yellow behind it goes grey, and a crude 'Saved!' winks.

options.name: Replace Colour
options.pitch: The person decides the picture is too busy and uses a Replace Colour tool. The less-used colour becomes the winner.
options.gives: The boldest visual: a whole-map takeover that reads instantly on a small screen.
options.costs: It hides how close a match was, so it may need a quick percentage first.
options.moment: A crude box asks 'Replace [orange] with [blue]?', the cursor clicks Yes, and the orange figures shrug and turn blue.

options.name: Undo To Grey
options.pitch: The person holds Undo and the match rewinds fast, draining each team's counter. Whichever colour lasts longer wins, and the bare grey canvas is the next match.
options.gives: The reveal and the rematch are one beat: the person tidies up the mess and unknowingly resets the game.
options.costs: It needs replay data, though the dev console's record/play is a head start.
options.moment: Paint peels back in fast reverse, pink hits zero first, and the slot goes green over a clean arena.

combos.name: Back Before Dinner
combos.flavour: warm, Toy Story, cosy secret life
combos.pitch: A kid draws the grey scene, gets called to dinner, and the outlined box-heads race to cover the picture in their colour so the kid will colour them in. You hear dinner going on in the next room, and footsteps end the match. The kid sits back down, hovers between the two swatches, drifts toward the one that covers more, and clicks.

combos.name: Unsaved Changes
combos.pitch: There is no story, only a program. The drawings live while the file is unsaved, an arrow sits parked in the corner, and the teams fight because of the caps they wear. Saving squeezes the picture into three colours and the loser goes grey, which is where all this grey came from.

combos.name: Lunch Hour Hang
combos.pitch: An office worker doodles on their lunch break, drags a colour into the empty slot, and the program hangs, splitting it into two copy-pasted crews who each claim to be the original. The busy spinner is the countdown, and the hang lasts one lunch hour. They come back, find a mess, and Replace Colour settles the argument.

combos.name: Grandad's Masterpiece
combos.pitch: Grandad has the colour picker open and cannot choose between two swatches, and his slow mouse hand drifts across the level as a platform. Each team wants to be the version that goes on the fridge. In the end he leans back, zooms out until it is all one colour, and is very proud of what he did.

clashes: away-from-desk / stuck-at-picker: the person cannot be both away from the desk and sitting at the colour picker (they are the same question, but stuck-at-picker also clashes with called-to-dinner, lunch-break and heard-not-seen for the same reason)
freeze-when-watched / heard-not-seen: one needs the person at the mouse, the other has them in another room
freeze-when-watched / drifting-arrow: the cursor cannot be both a freeze zone and a platform you ride
freeze-when-watched / screensaver-clock: the screen cannot idle off while someone is moving the mouse
not-responding / busy-countdown: with the hang, the spinner means the drawings are free; with the countdown, the spinner means they are frozen
person-in-on-it / fell-asleep: a person who knowingly referees cannot be asleep
person-in-on-it / heard-not-seen: a referee who is only heard from another room cannot drop weapons with the cursor
own-ink / paint-pet: paint cannot be both the figures' own body and a separate pet
undo-to-grey / make-the-fridge: undoing wipes the picture that was supposed to be kept
undo-to-grey / want-coloured-in: the rewind erases the picture just as the winners should be coloured in
only-cursor / called-to-dinner or heard-not-seen: an unasked, absent person cannot also be a kid or footsteps (if you pick only-cursor, presence must stay silent)
